newsitem.title: USA: Dow rallies, Republican-led Congress still seen.
newsitem.headline: Dow rallies, Republican-led Congress still seen.

text.p: U.S. stocks rallied as Wall Street grew more confident that the status quo would be maintained in Washington following the national elections, sending the long bond yield to a 7-1/2 month low.

"The market has predicted the election. It's jumped ahead and made the bet Republicans will retain control of Congress and (Democratic President Bill) Clinton will win re-election," said Prudential Securities' Larry Wachtel. "But if we're wrong dramatically, the Dow could fall 100-150 points" Wednesday.
The Dow industrials surged 40 points to about 6081.
That drew the blue chip index ever closer to its all-time closing high of 6094.23 set on October 18.
The S&P 500 index set an unofficial record closing high of 714.14, up seven. That eclipsed the previous record high finish of 710.82 set on October 18.
The Nasdaq Composite surged nine to 1229.
Winners outpaced losers 14-9 on very heavy NYSE volume of about 485 million shares.
The long bond rose 29/32 in late trading, knocking its yield down to 6.59 percent -- the lowest since March 26's close at a 6.58 percent yield.

"The market is celebrating a status quo election. There's also foreign buying of bonds and an unwinding of futures hedges in the S&Ps," said David Shulman, chief equity strategist at Salomon Brothers. "Status quo gives us the chance for entitlement reform." He noted the Dow has surged some 60 percent since Republicans won control of Congress two years ago. "The market obviously likes the current combination. If it's not broken, why fix it?"
Wall Street had been on edge in recent weeks, fearing a Democratic sweep might spur greater social spending, a ballooning deficit and a spike in inflation.

Interest-rate sensitive stocks led the market higher as the long bond yield headed south. Chase Manhattan rose 1-7/8 to 88-3/8 after setting a year-high of 88-7/8 intraday. Fannie Mae rose 5/8 to 38-1/4, Wells Fargo added 5-5/8 to 273-1/4 and Citicorp was up 1-3/4 to 101-1/4.

Drug stocks also firmed. "They've risen the past week or so with confidence there won't be a change in the composition of Congress," said Wachtel, a Prudential market analyst. Worries that a Democrat-led Congress would revisit health care reform had pressured the group. Merck rose 1/2 to 75-3/4, Pfizer added 1-7/8 to 86 and Eli Lilly rose 2-1/8 to 73-3/4.

Technology stocks were also solidly higher as worries about holiday PC sales abated, U.S. Robotics reported in-line quarterly results and Bear Stearns made bullish comments on Compaq. U.S. Robotics rose 1-1/2 to 61, Intel surged 3-5/8 to 114 after hitting a year-high 114-3/8, Microsoft rose 3-1/2 to a 52-week high of 141-1/2, Compaq rallied four to 70-3/8 and IBM rose 1-1/2 to 130-1/4.

Cisco Systems rose 1-1/8 to 61-3/4 ahead of its quarterly report. Ascend Communications, which will introduce a device to allow Internet providers to accept calls from higher speed 56-kilobit modems, surged 5-33/64 to 73-17/64.
Among individual shares, MCI Communications shares continued to fall, off 1-5/8 to 29-1/8 following the weekend news of a $20 billion plus merger with British Telecommunications.

Industry analysts cited MCI's changing role in a stock portfolio and a tight arbitrage opportunity may be partly to blame. "Previously MCI was a high growth U.S. long distance carrier," said Barry Sine of SBC Warburg. "Today if you buy MCI you are buying a call option on Britain's largest telephone company," he said.
Dow component Texaco lost three to 94-5/8.
Federal prosecutors launched a probe into whether some Texaco executives planned to destroy documents sought in a racial discrimination lawsuit, plaintiffs' lawyer said.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 8.59 to 1229.07.
The S&P 500 index rose 7.41 to 714.14, a record.
The NYSE Composite rose 3.36 to 378.43, a record.
(Figures official as of 1645 EST/2145 GMT)
-- Wall Street desk 212 859 1721.
